idiom_name: class with static data members (declared in class, defined in one .cpp)
implementation_notes: Make every data member static and keep the member functions non-static: a static data member is an independent object with static storage duration of which there is exactly one instance in the entire program, so every constructed instance reads and writes that same object while remaining cheap and copyable. The classic pre-C++17 form declares the member inside the class and defines it out of line in exactly one translation unit; since C++17 an inline static data member replaces that split (see the inline-static-cpp17 variant). Choose this form when initialization must happen in one controlled place or the code must still build as C++98/11/14.
pitfalls: A static data member is only declared inside the class: forget the out-of-class definition and you get a link error; define it twice and you break the ODR - the definition belongs in exactly one .cpp.

Static initialization happens before main() and the order across translation units is unspecified, so a monostate member initialized from another monostate can observe it uninitialized (the static initialization order fiasco).

Static storage is shared by all threads: make writes synchronized (an inline static std::mutex co-located with the data) and remember that const member functions reading static data still race with writers.

variants.name: C++17 inline static data members (header-only)
variants.idiom_name: inline static data member defined and initialized in class
variants.implementation_notes: Since C++17 a static data member may be declared inline, so it can be defined and initialized inside the class definition and no out-of-class definition is needed: the header stays self-contained and there is still exactly one object per program with external linkage. Prefer this variant for new code and header-only libraries; the static initialization order fiasco across translation units remains, because inline static members are initialized before main() in an unspecified order, so keep initializers constant or move non-trivial construction into a function-local static.
pitfalls: Inline static members are initialized before main() in an unspecified order across translation units, so non-constant initializers can still read an uninitialized monostate; use constant initializers or a function-local static.
Every translation unit including the header sees the same object, so a mixed build (one TU compiled as C++14) violates the ODR requirement that all definitions be identical.
The member is still mutable shared state: header visibility does not add synchronization.

variants.name: Function-local static accessor (lazy, exactly-once)
variants.idiom_name: static storage behind a function-local static accessor
variants.implementation_notes: When the data cannot be initialized before main() without risking the static initialization order fiasco, keep the ordinary instance interface but back it with a function-local static: C++11 guarantees that such a variable is initialized exactly once, thread-safely, on first use, and destroyed at exit. The instance interface stays ordinary; what changes is that the storage is created lazily, so this monostate may depend on other monostates' state without ordering hazards. Use it when initialization is expensive or depends on runtime configuration.
pitfalls: Initialization is thread-safe, the initialized object is not: the vector returned by the accessor still needs external synchronization for concurrent writes.
Destruction order at exit is unspecified (static destruction order fiasco): another static object's destructor may use the monostate after it has been destroyed.
The accessor must stay the only door to the storage - calling it from several places is fine, but caching its address in another static reintroduces the ordering problem.
